title: Prefer array_first() and array_last()
summary: PHP 8.5 added array_first() and array_last(), which read an array's first and last values without touching its internal pointer, replacing the older reset()/end() and array_key_first()/array_key_last() indexing idioms for that purpose.
new_code_policy: On a feature ceiling of 8.5 or above, prefer array_first($array) / array_last($array) over reset($array)/end($array) or array_key_first()/array_key_last()-based indexing when the goal is only to read the first or last value.
existing_code_policy: Once the project's PHP floor reaches 8.5, existing reset()/end() or array_key_first()/array_key_last()-indexing calls that merely read the first/last value can be replaced incrementally with array_first()/array_last(); leave alone any call site where the code also relies on reset()/end() moving the array's internal pointer for a later next()/current()/key() call, or on the false-vs-empty-value return of reset()/end() on an empty array, since array_first()/array_last() do neither.
guideline: Use array_first($array) / array_last($array) to read the first or last element of an array instead of reset()/end() or $array[array_key_first($array)] / $array[array_key_last($array)] indexing, unless the code specifically needs the array-pointer side effect that reset()/end() also produce.
details: PHP 8.5 added array_first($array) and array_last($array) to the Standard extension (RFC array_first_last): each returns the first or last value of $array, or null when $array is empty, and neither touches the array's internal pointer. Before 8.5, the idiomatic ways to read the first or last value were reset($array)/end($array) -- which move the internal pointer as a side effect and return false, not null, on an empty array -- or index-based access such as $array[array_key_first($array)] ?? null. 8.5 is the minor array_first()/array_last() became available, not a claim about the older reset()/end() idiom this rule replaces.
notes: array_first()/array_last() return null for an empty array and never move the array's internal pointer, unlike reset()/end(), which return false on an empty array and move the pointer to the first/last element as a side effect -- a blind replacement is unsafe wherever that pointer movement or the false return value is relied upon elsewhere.

array_key_first($array) !== null / array_key_last($array) !== null remain the correct way to check whether an array has any elements at all when the key itself is also needed; array_first()/array_last() only ever hand back the value.
